title: Crestone Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Crestone wells have a 105 ft median depth; see local yields, water levels, drilling costs, risks and permit history.
h1: Crestone, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
For a rural property near Crestone, the well records point to relatively shallow drilling in many locations, but the ground is not uniform. The median permitted well is 105 feet deep, and the middle half runs from 55 to 150 feet. Reported well yields are generally useful for household supply, with a median of 12.2 gallons per minute. Those figures come from permitted wells within five miles of Crestone, not a guarantee for a particular lot.

The records also include fractured-bedrock wells and San Luis Valley aquifer wells. Before buying land or setting a building site, review nearby permits, confirm the water-rights situation, and have a driller evaluate access, geology, casing, grout, pump sizing, and septic layout.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Crestone?
sections.html:
Crestone's well depths vary, but the local record is weighted toward shallow and moderate drilling. Forty percent of reported wells are under 100 feet, while 57% fall between 100 and 300 feet. The middle half is 55 to 150 feet, making a median-depth bid a useful starting point rather than a promise.

The deepest recorded well is 1,235 feet, and 3% are between 300 and 600 feet, with 1% at 600 feet or deeper. Crestone permits commonly identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, while others name the Unconfined San Luis Valley aquifer. Mixed sedimentary, alluvial, and fractured ground can change the drilling plan quickly. Ask for a written allowance covering extra depth, casing, grout, and difficult access.

sections.heading: What water yield can a Crestone well provide?
sections.html:
The reported yield picture is favorable for ordinary household use, with an observed median of 12.2 gallons per minute and a middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty percent of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 37% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Only 188 wells report a pump yield, so this is not a result for every permitted well. The records show 0% under 1 gallon per minute and 3% from 1 to 5 gallons per minute, but a buyer should still verify the specific well's production and recovery. A driller can discuss pump testing, storage, and the difference between a measured yield and dependable long-term supply. Colorado exempt household-use wells have a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Is the water table changing near Crestone?
sections.html:
Reported static water levels are fairly shallow. The median depth to water is 35 feet, with the middle half from 20 to 59 feet. That matters for pump placement, trenching, and the amount of casing and equipment a contractor may recommend, but a nearby measurement is more useful than the regional median for a specific parcel.

The decade series does not show a dropping water table in these records. The median static level was 38 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 35 feet in the 2020s, meaning the later median is slightly shallower. Only 68 wells report a static water level, and measurement conditions differ, so this should be read as a limited local indication rather than a long-term basin study.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Crestone, and when?
sections.html:
The permit history shows sustained drilling activity, especially from the 1990s onward. Permits issued by decade include 205 in the 1990s, 173 in the 2000s, 129 in the 2010s, and 85 in the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2026. Most permitted use is domestic or household supply at 81%, followed by stock at 10%, monitoring at 8%, and irrigation at 3%.

The most active names in these records are Heersink Drilling (Heersink, Scott) with 91 wells, Nwp Drlg & Consul (Newmyer, Halsey R.) with 69, and Valley Pump Company (Self, Clinton L.) with 40. Treat this as permit history, not a current recommendation or availability list.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost in Crestone?
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground described in the local cost model, a typical drilling rate is $50 to $75 per foot. At the local median depth of 105 feet, the drilled hole alone models to about $5,200 to $7,900. That figure is not the complete water system.

A finished well, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, models to about $11,200 to $19,900 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, or changes in the pump and storage design can move the bid outside that range. When comparing proposals, ask what is included, how extra footage is priced, and whether the estimate covers permits, testing, electrical service, and connection to the planned house.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Crestone
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main pattern in the reported data, but the sample is incomplete and geology can change from one lot to the next. Fractured granite or other fractured bedrock can be unpredictable, including the possibility of drilling deeper than nearby wells or encountering a dry hole. Review neighboring permits and ask a driller to interpret actual logs, not just advertised averages.

Water quality also needs a parcel-specific test. The mapped area has 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site and 68 historic mine features within about 10 miles. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that mapped area. Those facts do not establish the quality of a particular well. Test the existing or new well, confirm casing and grout, and keep septic setbacks, drainfield space, slope, access, and the house site coordinated before excavation.

sections.heading: Buying land or planning a new well in Crestone
sections.html:
Start with the well permit and construction record for the parcel, then compare it with nearby records in Crestone and surrounding areas such as Moffat, Westcliffe, Silver Cliff, Hooper, Saguache, and Mosca. Look for depth, aquifer description, static water level, yield, and intended use. A permit is not the same as a guaranteed water supply, and a vacant parcel may need a new Colorado Division of Water Resources permit and a qualified driller's site review.

For a building project, secure access for the rig, identify the likely well location, and reserve room for the septic system, replacement drainfield, utility trench, and driveway. If the basin is over-appropriated, confirm whether an augmentation plan or other water-supply requirement applies. Get a written drilling allowance and separate bids for the complete system, then make the purchase contract contingent on the water and septic findings you need.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Crestone, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well near Crestone is 105 feet deep, and the middle half runs from 55 to 150 feet. Forty percent are under 100 feet, while 57% are between 100 and 300 feet. Depth still varies substantially: the deepest recorded well is 1,235 feet, so nearby well logs matter more than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Crestone?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 105-foot median depth, drilling the hole models to about $5,200 to $7,900. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical models to about $11,200 to $19,900. Difficult access, extra depth, casing, grout, and site conditions can change the final bid.

faq.q: Do Crestone wells produce enough water for a house?
faq.a: Reported yields have a median of 12.2 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty percent produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 37% report more than 15. Only 188 wells report yield, so require testing and review of the specific well before relying on the data.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Crestone?
faq.a: The regional permit records do not prove that any individual well is safe to drink. There is 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site and 68 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the parcel's water for relevant contaminants, especially before buying, building, or using an older well.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Crestone?
faq.a: The limited reported measurements do not show a dropping trend. Median static water level was 38 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 35 feet in the 2020s, which is slightly shallower in the later decade. Only 68 wells report static water levels, and different measurement conditions mean this is not a complete groundwater study.
